title: Light: Mirrors and Lenses
subject: Science
description: Concave and convex mirrors and the images they form, the two laws of reflection, converging and diverging of light by spherical mirrors and lenses, concentrating sunlight, and everyday uses of mirrors and lenses.

questions.question: At the science centre Meena's face looked unusually large in a curved mirror, while her brother, standing farther away, appeared upside down. Which kind of mirror was it?
options: A concave mirror
A convex mirror
A plane mirror
A flat glass pane
questions.explanation: Only a concave mirror gives an enlarged erect image for a near object and an inverted image for a far object. A convex mirror always gives a small erect image and a plane mirror gives a same-size image.

questions.question: Spherical mirrors are shaped like a part of which imaginary object?
options: A hollow glass tube
A hollow glass sphere
A solid glass cube
A flat glass sheet
questions.explanation: The chapter defines spherical mirrors as curved mirrors shaped like a part of a hollow glass sphere; their reflecting surfaces are spherical.

questions.question: A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves inwards is called a
options: plane mirror
bulging mirror
concave mirror
convex mirror
questions.explanation: A reflecting surface curved inwards (like the inside of a spoon) makes a concave mirror; a surface curved outwards makes a convex mirror.

questions.question: Which mirror has a reflecting surface that bulges outwards?
options: Concave mirror
Plane mirror
Dental mirror
Convex mirror
questions.explanation: A convex mirror's reflecting surface curves outwards, like the back of a spoon. The dental mirror is concave.

questions.question: You look at your face in the inner, inward-curving side of a shiny spoon held near your face and then move it slowly away. What do you notice about the image?
options: It is inverted when the spoon is farther away
It stays erect and the same size throughout
It is erect and smaller at every distance
It disappears completely once the spoon moves
questions.explanation: The inner side of a spoon acts like a concave mirror: close up the image is erect and enlarged, and as the spoon moves away the image becomes inverted (Fig. 10.1a).

questions.question: When Meena flips the spoon and looks at its outer, bulging side, the image of her face is
options: inverted and smaller than her face
erect but smaller than her face
inverted and larger than her face
erect and the same size as her face
questions.explanation: The outer side of the spoon acts like a convex mirror, which always forms an erect, diminished image (Fig. 10.1b).

questions.question: Spherical mirrors are manufactured by slicing a hollow glass sphere into pieces.
questions.explanation: False. The sphere is only an imaginary way to think about the shape. Real spherical mirrors are made by grinding and polishing a flat piece of glass into a curved surface and then coating it.

questions.question: A curved glass piece is coated with a thin reflective layer on its OUTER curved surface. What does it become?
options: A convex lens
A plane mirror
A concave mirror
A convex mirror
questions.explanation: Light reflects from the uncoated side. With the coating on the outer (bulging) surface, the reflecting face is the inner, inward-curving surface, so the piece is a concave mirror.

questions.question: If the reflective coating is applied on the INNER curved surface of the glass piece instead, the mirror formed is
options: concave, reflecting from its inner surface
plane, because the coating flattens it
a lens, because light passes through
convex, reflecting from its outer surface
questions.explanation: Coating the inner surface leaves the outer, outward-bulging surface to reflect light, which is the definition of a convex mirror.

questions.question: In the schematic drawing of a concave or convex mirror, what does the shaded part represent?
options: The non-reflecting back surface
The reflecting front surface
The imaginary hollow sphere
The thin aluminium coating only
questions.explanation: In the representations (Fig. 10.2b and 10.3b) the non-reflecting surface of the mirror is shown shaded, so the unshaded side is the reflecting side.

questions.question: In Activity 10.2, how do students tell a concave mirror from a convex one WITHOUT looking at any image?
options: Look into it from a few metres away
View the mirror from the side at eye level
Compare the thickness of middle and edges
Shine a torch on it and watch the reflected beam
questions.explanation: Placing the mirrors reflecting-side up and viewing them edge-on at eye level shows whether the surface curves inwards (concave) or outwards (convex). Thickness comparison is how lenses are told apart.

questions.question: The outline of the surface of a spherical mirror is circular.
questions.explanation: True. The chapter notes that the outline of a spherical mirror's surface is circular, because it is a piece of a sphere.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements that correctly describe spherical mirrors.
options: Their reflecting surface is part of a sphere
They are made by grinding and polishing flat glass
They are cut from a real hollow glass sphere
Their reflecting surface is always coated on the inside
questions.explanation: Spherical mirrors have spherical reflecting surfaces and are made by grinding and polishing a flat glass piece. They are not sliced from a sphere, and the coating side decides whether they are concave (outer coated) or convex (inner coated).

questions.question: Meena sees an inverted image of her face in a spoon held at arm's length. She flips the spoon over without changing the distance. What does she see now?
options: An erect image the same size as her face
No image, since the back is not shiny
An erect, smaller image of her face
An inverted, larger image of her face
questions.explanation: Flipping the spoon swaps the concave inner side for the convex outer side. The convex side always gives an erect, diminished image, whatever the distance.

questions.question: Which material does the chapter give as an example of the thin reflective coating used to make a spherical mirror?
options: Chromium
Mercury
Graphite
Aluminium
questions.explanation: The chapter says a reflective coating 'like a thin layer of aluminium' is applied to the curved glass surface to make the mirror.

questions.question: An object is placed very close to a concave mirror. Its image is
options: erect and enlarged
erect and diminished
inverted and enlarged
inverted and diminished
questions.explanation: Close to a concave mirror the image is erect and larger than the object; it becomes inverted only when the object is moved farther away.

questions.question: An object is moved steadily away from a concave mirror. Which sequence of images is observed?
options: Erect same size at all distances, then inverted at the end
Erect enlarged, then inverted enlarged, then inverted smaller
Erect enlarged, then erect smaller, then inverted smaller
Inverted smaller, then inverted enlarged, then erect enlarged
questions.explanation: The chapter says the near image is erect and enlarged; on moving the object away the image becomes inverted, is initially enlarged and then keeps getting smaller.

questions.question: In a museum a woman walks TOWARDS a large concave mirror from far away. She will see that
options: her inverted image keeps shrinking all the way up to the mirror
her erect image keeps growing all the way up to the mirror
her inverted image grows, finally turning erect and magnified
her erect image keeps shrinking all the way up to the mirror
questions.explanation: Walking towards the mirror reverses the sequence seen when moving away: far away the image is inverted and small, it grows as she approaches, and close to the mirror it becomes erect and magnified.

questions.question: Which statement about images formed by a concave mirror is NOT correct?
options: The image can be larger than the object
The image can be smaller than the object
The image can be upside down (inverted)
The image is erect at every object distance
questions.explanation: A concave mirror's image may be enlarged, diminished or the same size, and erect or inverted, depending on the object's distance — it is not always erect.

questions.question: The image formed by a concave mirror can be enlarged, diminished or of the same size as the object.
questions.explanation: True. The Snapshots list says a concave mirror's image can be enlarged, diminished or same size, erect or inverted, depending on the object distance.

questions.question: In a concave mirror the image becomes inverted when the object is brought very close to the mirror.
questions.explanation: False. It is the opposite: close to the mirror the image is erect and enlarged; it becomes inverted when the object is moved farther away.

questions.question: In Activity 10.3 a toy kept 3–4 cm from a concave mirror gives an erect enlarged image. The toy is slowly moved to the far end of the table. The image finally seen is
options: inverted and smaller than the toy
erect and smaller than the toy
inverted and larger than the toy
erect and larger than the toy
questions.explanation: After the image inverts it is first enlarged and then keeps getting smaller, so at a large distance the image is inverted and diminished.

questions.question: A dentist's concave mirror shows an enlarged view of a tooth only when it is held close to the tooth. What would happen if it were held far from the tooth?
options: No image would form at that distance
The tooth would appear inverted
The tooth would appear erect and even larger
The tooth would look the same size as it is
questions.explanation: A concave mirror gives an erect enlarged image only for a nearby object; for a farther object the image turns inverted, which is useless for examining teeth.

questions.question: What decides whether a concave mirror forms an erect or an inverted image of an object?
options: The thickness of the glass of the mirror
The brightness of the light in the room
The distance of the object from the mirror
The colour of the object placed before it
questions.explanation: The chapter repeatedly stresses that for a concave mirror the size and orientation of the image depend on the object's distance from the mirror.

questions.question: Which TWO of these images can a concave mirror form?
options: Erect and enlarged, when the object is close
Inverted and smaller, when the object is far
Erect and the same size at every distance
Inverted and enlarged, when the object is very close
questions.explanation: Near objects give an erect enlarged image and far objects an inverted diminished one. A same-size image at every distance is a plane mirror property, and very close objects do not give inverted images.

questions.question: Why did Meena's brother, who stood a little farther from the curved mirror than Meena, appear upside down?
options: He was walking, so the moving image flipped as he passed
The mirror was convex and convex mirrors invert distant objects
The mirror was tilted and laterally inverted his image
He was far enough from the concave mirror to be inverted
questions.explanation: A concave mirror inverts the image of an object placed farther away, while a nearby object (Meena) gives an erect enlarged image. Convex mirrors never invert.

questions.question: In Fig. 10.25 a graph sheet is placed before three mirrors. In one mirror its squares look inverted and enlarged. That mirror is
options: concave
convex
plane
flat glass
questions.explanation: Only a concave mirror can produce an inverted image; a convex mirror gives a small erect image and a plane mirror an erect same-size image.

questions.question: A concave mirror can form an image that is exactly the same size as the object.
questions.explanation: True. The Snapshots state that the image in a concave mirror can be enlarged, diminished OR of the same size as the object.

questions.question: Which single mirror can show you BOTH an erect image and an inverted image of the same object, just by changing its distance?
options: Side-view mirror
Concave mirror
Convex mirror
Plane mirror
questions.explanation: Only the concave mirror changes from erect (object near) to inverted (object far). Convex and plane mirrors (and a convex side-view mirror) always give erect images.

questions.question: The image formed by a convex mirror is always
options: inverted and diminished
inverted and enlarged
erect and diminished
erect and enlarged
questions.explanation: Whatever the object distance, a convex mirror forms an erect image smaller than the object.

questions.question: As an object is moved AWAY from a convex mirror, the size of its image
options: increases slightly but stays erect
stays exactly the same size
first grows and then becomes inverted
decreases slightly but stays erect
questions.explanation: The chapter says the convex-mirror image is always erect and diminished, and its size decreases slightly as the object is moved away.

questions.question: A convex mirror forms an inverted image when the object is placed far from it.
questions.explanation: False. A convex mirror never inverts; its image is erect and diminished for every object distance.

questions.question: Which statement about a convex mirror is NOT correct?
options: Its image grows larger as the object moves away
Its image is erect for every object distance
Its image is always smaller than the object
It shows lateral inversion like other mirrors
questions.explanation: The image of a convex mirror is always diminished and actually shrinks slightly as the object moves away. It is erect and, like all mirrors, laterally inverted.

questions.question: At one mirror in the science centre Meena saw a tiny, upright version of herself. That mirror was
options: a magnifying glass
a convex mirror
a concave mirror
a plane mirror
questions.explanation: An erect, diminished image is the signature of a convex mirror. A concave mirror would enlarge or invert, and a plane mirror keeps the size the same.

questions.question: In a vehicle's side-view mirror the traffic behind appears
options: inverted and smaller than actual size
inverted and the same size as actual
erect and smaller than actual size
erect and larger than actual size
questions.explanation: Side-view mirrors are convex, so they always form an erect image smaller than the actual vehicles.

questions.question: Side-view mirrors carry the warning 'Objects in mirror are closer than they appear'. Why is this warning needed?
options: Lateral inversion places vehicles on the wrong side
The curved glass slows the light reaching the eye
The erect image hides the vehicle's actual position
The diminished image makes vehicles look farther away
questions.explanation: A convex mirror makes the image smaller than the object; small images are judged to be farther away, so drivers may underestimate how close the vehicle behind really is.

questions.question: In the matching exercise, 'It forms an image which is always erect and diminished in size' describes which item?
options: Convex mirror
Concave mirror
Convex lens
Plane mirror
questions.explanation: Of the mirrors listed, only the convex mirror always gives an erect, diminished image. A concave lens behaves similarly but is a lens, not a mirror.

questions.question: The size of the image in a convex mirror decreases slightly as the object is moved away from it.
questions.explanation: True. The chapter notes that although the convex-mirror image is always erect and smaller, its size decreases slightly as the object moves away.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements that are true for an image formed by a convex mirror.
options: The image is erect for every object distance
The image is always smaller than the object
The image is enlarged when the object is very close
The image turns upside down for distant objects
questions.explanation: A convex mirror always produces an erect, diminished image. Enlargement near the mirror and inversion for distant objects are concave-mirror behaviours.

questions.question: A shopper walks TOWARDS a convex surveillance mirror in a store. How does her image change?
options: It grows until it is larger than her near the mirror
It stays erect and grows slightly, yet stays smaller
It stays erect and shrinks, becoming tinier than before
It becomes inverted once she comes close enough to it
questions.explanation: Moving away makes the convex image slightly smaller, so moving closer makes it slightly larger, yet it is always erect and always diminished.

questions.question: Compared with a plane mirror of the same size, a convex side-view mirror shows
options: exactly the same area of the road behind
only the area directly behind the vehicle
a much wider area of the road behind
a much narrower area of the road behind
questions.explanation: Because the convex mirror is curved outwards, it provides a much wider view of the road behind than a plane mirror would.

questions.question: A plane mirror always forms an image that is
options: erect and smaller than the object
inverted and the same size as the object
erect and larger than the object
erect and the same size as the object
questions.explanation: A plane mirror always forms an erect image of the same size as the object, unlike spherical mirrors whose image size changes with distance.

questions.question: Lateral inversion of the image is seen in
options: plane, concave and convex mirrors alike
plane mirrors only, not curved ones
concave mirrors only, not plane or convex
convex and plane mirrors but not concave
questions.explanation: The chapter states that lateral inversion of the image is seen in all three types of mirrors.

questions.question: Lateral inversion occurs only in plane mirrors, not in spherical mirrors.
questions.explanation: False. Lateral inversion is seen in all three types of mirrors — plane, concave and convex.

questions.question: A sketch-pen cap is placed in front of three mirrors. Image (i) is erect and the same size, image (ii) is erect and enlarged, image (iii) is erect and smaller. The correct matching is
options: (i) convex, (ii) concave, (iii) plane
(i) plane, (ii) concave, (iii) convex
(i) plane, (ii) convex, (iii) concave
(i) concave, (ii) plane, (iii) convex
questions.explanation: Same-size erect image means plane mirror; an erect enlarged image of a near object means concave mirror; an erect diminished image means convex mirror.

questions.question: How can you identify whether a mirror is plane, concave or convex simply by using a small object?
options: Check whether the object's colours are reversed in the image
See whether the image is laterally inverted or not
Watch how the image's size and orientation change with distance
Measure how heavy the mirror is compared with the object
questions.explanation: Image size stays fixed in a plane mirror, changes and may invert in a concave mirror, and stays small and erect in a convex mirror. Lateral inversion happens in all three, so it cannot distinguish them.

questions.question: In which mirror does the image size NOT change as the object is moved towards or away from it?
options: Concave mirror
Convex mirror
Dental mirror
Plane mirror
questions.explanation: A plane mirror's image is always the same size as the object. In concave and convex mirrors (and a dental mirror is concave) the size changes with the object's distance.

questions.question: Two diagrams show an object O, a mirror M and its image I. In diagram (a) the image is erect and the same size as O; in diagram (b) it is erect and smaller than O. The mirrors are
options: (a) plane mirror and (b) convex mirror
(a) convex mirror and (b) concave mirror
(a) plane mirror and (b) concave mirror
(a) concave mirror and (b) convex mirror
questions.explanation: An erect same-size image is formed only by a plane mirror, and an erect diminished image only by a convex mirror.

questions.question: In which type of mirror does the image become inverted when the object is taken farther away?
options: Side-view mirror
Concave mirror
Convex mirror
Plane mirror
questions.explanation: Only a concave mirror inverts the image when the object is moved away; plane and convex (side-view) mirrors always give erect images.

questions.question: Which TWO statements are true for ALL three types of mirrors — plane, concave and convex?
options: The image shows lateral inversion
The laws of reflection are obeyed
The image size stays the same as the object moves
A parallel beam stays parallel after reflection
questions.explanation: Lateral inversion is seen in all three mirrors and the laws of reflection hold for every mirror. Constant image size and parallel reflected beams are true only for plane mirrors.

questions.question: In Fig. 10.25 three unlabelled mirrors reflect a graph sheet: mirror X shows the squares the same size, mirror Y shows them enlarged and inverted, mirror Z shows them smaller and erect. Mirror Z is
options: plane
flat glass
convex
concave
questions.explanation: A smaller erect image identifies a convex mirror; X (same size) is plane and Y (inverted, enlarged) is concave.

questions.question: A plane mirror always forms an erect image of the same size as the object.
questions.explanation: True. This is the plane-mirror property recalled from Grade 7 and contrasted with spherical mirrors in this chapter.

questions.question: A student says: 'My image was erect and smaller, so the mirror must be concave.' What is the error?
options: An erect, smaller image is formed by a plane mirror
A concave mirror cannot form an erect image at all
A concave mirror never forms a smaller image
An erect, smaller image is formed by a convex mirror
questions.explanation: Erect and diminished is the signature of a convex mirror. A concave mirror gives an erect image only when it is enlarged (object close), and a plane mirror never changes the size.

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: The reflectors of torches and the headlights of cars and scooters are
options: concave in shape
convex in shape
plane in shape
flat glass plates
questions.explanation: Torch reflectors and vehicle headlights use concave mirrors (Fig. 10.6a).

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: A dentist's mirror gives an enlarged view of the teeth. It is a
options: convex lens held far from the teeth
concave mirror held close to the teeth
convex mirror held close to the teeth
plane mirror held far from the teeth
questions.explanation: A dental mirror is a concave mirror; held close to the teeth it provides an erect, enlarged view (Fig. 10.6b).

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: The side-view mirrors on vehicles are
options: plane mirrors
convex lenses
convex mirrors
concave mirrors
questions.explanation: Side-view mirrors are convex: they give an erect, smaller image of the traffic behind and a wide field of view.

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: Why are convex mirrors installed at road intersections and sharp bends?
options: So drivers see an enlarged image of oncoming traffic
So sunlight is concentrated to light up the bend at night
So drivers see an inverted view that is easier to judge
So drivers on both sides can see each other and avoid collisions
questions.explanation: The wide view of a convex mirror lets drivers approaching from both sides see what is coming around the bend, preventing collisions (Fig. 10.7b).

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: Big stores install convex mirrors mainly to
options: monitor a large area and deter thefts
magnify the goods on display for customers
concentrate light onto the shelves
give customers a same-size view of themselves
questions.explanation: A convex mirror covers a much wider area, so a single mirror lets staff watch a large part of the store and discourages theft (Fig. 10.7c).

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: In most modern reflecting telescopes, the main mirror is a
options: large convex lens
large concave mirror
large convex mirror
large plane mirror
questions.explanation: The 'A step further' box says most modern telescopes are reflecting telescopes whose main mirror is a large concave mirror.

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: Assertion: Convex mirrors are preferred for observing the traffic behind us. Reason: Convex mirrors provide a significantly larger view area than plane mirrors. Choose the correct option.
options: The Assertion is correct but the Reason given is incorrect
Both the Assertion and the Reason given are incorrect
Both are correct and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Both are correct but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors are used as side-view mirrors precisely because, being curved outwards, they show a much wider area of the road behind than a plane mirror would.

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: Why would a concave mirror be a poor choice as a vehicle's side-view mirror?
options: It would make distant vehicles look too small to notice
It would show vehicles on the wrong side of the road
It cannot reflect light coming from behind the vehicle
Distant vehicles would appear inverted and the view would be narrow
questions.explanation: A concave mirror inverts the image of far-away objects and does not provide the wide view a convex mirror gives, so it would confuse the driver.

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: Select the TWO devices that use a CONCAVE mirror.
options: Reflector of a torch
Dentist's mirror
Vehicle side-view mirror
Store surveillance mirror
questions.explanation: Torch reflectors and dental mirrors are concave. Side-view and store surveillance mirrors are convex because they need a wide, erect view.

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: Convex mirrors are used as torch reflectors because they spread the light over a wide area.
questions.explanation: False. Torch reflectors are concave mirrors; they converge light rather than spreading it. Convex mirrors are used in side-view and surveillance mirrors.

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: Convex mirrors are installed at sharp bends so that drivers from both sides can see the other side of the bend.
questions.explanation: True. Convex road-safety mirrors give drivers on both sides a view of the other side and help prevent collisions.

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: An ENT specialist or dentist wants a mirror that shows an enlarged view of a tooth or the inside of the throat. The most suitable mirror is a
options: concave mirror held close to the part
convex mirror held close to the part
plane mirror held at any distance
concave mirror held far from the part
questions.explanation: The chapter shows that a dental mirror is concave and gives an enlarged view when held close; held far it would invert the image.

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: In which of these uses must the object be CLOSE to the mirror for the mirror to do its job?
options: A surveillance mirror in a big store
A dentist examining a tooth
A side-view mirror on a scooter
A convex mirror at a sharp road bend
questions.explanation: The dental concave mirror enlarges only a nearby object. The other three are convex mirrors, which work for distant objects and give erect diminished images.

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: Which property of a convex mirror makes it useful for surveillance in big stores?
options: It inverts the image of distant shoppers
It concentrates light on the shelves
It shows a very wide area in one mirror
It makes shoppers appear enlarged
questions.explanation: Because a convex mirror covers a much wider area, one mirror lets staff watch a large part of the store.

questions.topic: Uses of Concave and Convex Mirrors
questions.question: Select the TWO uses that depend on a mirror providing a WIDE field of view.
options: Side-view mirror on a vehicle
Surveillance mirror in a store
Reflector inside a torch
Main mirror of a reflecting telescope
questions.explanation: Side-view and surveillance mirrors are convex and are chosen for the wide area they show. Torch reflectors and telescope main mirrors are concave and are used to converge light.

questions.question: Light is often represented by straight lines with arrows. These lines are called
options: beams
normals
slits
rays
questions.explanation: Rays are straight lines with arrows that indicate the path along which light travels.

questions.question: The ray of light that falls on a mirror is called the
options: incident ray
reflected ray
normal ray
refracted ray
questions.explanation: The ray falling on the mirror is the incident ray; the ray coming back from the mirror is the reflected ray.

questions.question: The ray of light that comes back from the mirror after striking it is the
options: emergent ray
reflected ray
incident ray
normal line
questions.explanation: The returning ray is the reflected ray. The normal is the perpendicular line drawn at the point of incidence, not a ray of light.

questions.question: The 'normal' to a mirror at the point of incidence is a line drawn
options: along the path of the incident ray
halfway between the incident and reflected rays
at 90° to the mirror surface at that point
along the mirror surface through that point
questions.explanation: The normal is the line making an angle of 90° with the mirror at the point where the incident ray strikes it.

questions.question: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and
options: the surface of the mirror
the reflected ray
the table on which the mirror stands
the normal at the point of incidence
questions.explanation: Angles of incidence and reflection are both measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface.

questions.question: A student finds that the reflected ray makes 60° with the mirror SURFACE. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.explanation: The angle of reflection is measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror. 90° − 60° = 30°.

questions.question: In Fig. 10.9 the letter O marks the
options: position of the observer's eye in the diagram
point where the incident ray hits the mirror
centre of the mirror's imaginary sphere
point where the reflected ray leaves the paper
questions.explanation: O is the point of incidence — the point on the mirror where the incident ray strikes and from which the normal is drawn.

questions.question: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the surface of the mirror.
questions.explanation: False. The angle of incidence is measured between the incident ray and the NORMAL to the mirror at the point of incidence.

questions.question: An incident ray makes an angle of 25° with the surface of a plane mirror. The angle of incidence is
questions.explanation: The normal is perpendicular to the mirror, so the angle with the normal is 90° − 25° = 65°.

questions.question: Why can the path of light be drawn as a straight line with an arrow?
options: Light always travels horizontally
Light bends only inside mirrors
Light moves in waves that look straight
Light travels along a straight line
questions.explanation: The chapter reminds us that light travels along a straight line, so its path can be shown by a straight ray.

questions.question: In Activity 10.4 all the openings of a comb except one in the middle are covered with black paper. What is the purpose?
options: To obtain a single thin beam of light
To obtain many parallel beams of light
To darken the room for a clearer image
To make the comb act like a plane mirror
questions.explanation: Covering all but one slit gives one thin beam along the paper. In Activity 10.6 many openings are left open to get multiple parallel beams instead.

questions.question: Select the TWO angles that are measured from the NORMAL.
options: Angle of incidence
Angle of reflection
Angle between incident ray and mirror
Angle between the mirror and the table
questions.explanation: Both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are defined with respect to the normal at the point of incidence.

questions.question: What do rays in a diagram indicate?
options: The speed at which light moves
The path along which light travels
The brightness of the light source
The colour of the reflected light
questions.explanation: Rays are straight lines with arrows showing the path along which light travels.

questions.question: According to the first law of reflection,
options: the angle of incidence plus reflection equals 90°
the reflected ray is always perpendicular to the mirror
the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
the angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection
questions.explanation: Careful measurement in Activity 10.4 shows that the angle of incidence (i) is equal to the angle of reflection (r).

questions.question: The second law of reflection states that the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence
options: are always at right angles to each other
all pass through the centre of the mirror
lie in three different planes
all lie in the same plane
questions.explanation: The incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane — demonstrated by the bent-paper Activity 10.5.

questions.question: A light ray strikes a mirror making 40° with the normal. What angle does the REFLECTED ray make with the MIRROR?
questions.explanation: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 40° from the normal. The angle with the mirror surface is 90° − 40° = 50°.

questions.question: When light is incident along the normal to a mirror, which statement is true?
options: No reflection of light takes place
The angle of incidence is 0°
The angle of incidence is 90°
The angle of reflection is 90°
questions.explanation: A ray along the normal makes 0° with it, so both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are zero and the ray is reflected back along the same path.

questions.question: A mirror is tilted and a light ray falls on it at 20° from the normal to the tilted surface. The angle of reflection is
questions.explanation: The law i = r holds whatever the tilt of the mirror, so the reflected ray also makes 20° with the normal.

questions.question: A mirror is tilted, but the light ray still falls along the normal to the tilted surface. The reflected ray
options: is reflected at the tilt angle of the mirror
travels along the surface of the tilted mirror
is reflected at 90° to the incident ray's direction
retraces its path, with angle of reflection 0°
questions.explanation: Tilting the mirror does not matter if the ray is along the new normal: angle of incidence is 0°, so the angle of reflection is 0° and the ray retraces its path.

questions.question: In Activity 10.5 the reflected beam disappears from the chart paper when the extended part of the paper is bent down over the table edge. This demonstrates that
options: the reflected ray lies in the plane of the incident ray
the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence
light cannot travel along a bent sheet of paper
the mirror stops reflecting when the paper is bent
questions.explanation: Bending the sheet creates a new plane, breaking the alignment, so the reflected beam no longer appears on it. The beam reappears when the paper is flattened — the second law of reflection.

questions.question: In Activity 10.5, what exactly does bending the sheet of paper do?
options: It moves the normal away from the point of incidence
It creates a new plane that excludes the reflected beam
It changes the angle of incidence of the light beam
It blocks the torch light from reaching the mirror
questions.explanation: The bent portion is a different plane from the one containing the incident ray and normal, so the reflected beam, which lies in the original plane, is not seen on it.

questions.question: For which mirrors are the laws of reflection valid?
options: Concave mirrors only
Plane and convex mirrors, not concave
Plane, concave and convex mirrors
Plane mirrors only
questions.explanation: The laws of reflection are valid for all kinds of mirrors — plane and spherical (both concave and convex).

questions.question: When a ray falls along the normal, both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are 0°.
questions.explanation: True. The ray coincides with the normal, so both angles are zero and the ray is reflected back along its own path.

questions.question: The laws of reflection apply to plane mirrors only and not to curved mirrors.
questions.explanation: False. Each ray obeys the laws of reflection on plane, concave and convex mirrors alike; the curved shape just makes parallel rays converge or diverge.

questions.question: A ray strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. The angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is
questions.explanation: The reflected ray makes 35° with the normal on the other side, so the two rays are 35° + 35° = 70° apart.

questions.question: In Activity 10.4 the torch and slit are moved so the beam falls at a different angle on the mirror. What happens to the reflected beam?
options: It shifts so its angle with the normal equals the new angle i
It stays in exactly the same direction as it was before
It shifts to make a fixed 90° angle with the incident beam
It disappears until the original angle of incidence is restored
questions.explanation: Since i = r always, changing the angle of incidence changes the direction of the reflected beam by the same amount (Fig. 10.8).

questions.question: Select the TWO statements that are laws of reflection.
options: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The incident ray, normal and reflected ray lie in one plane
The angle of incidence and angle of reflection add up to 90°
The reflected ray is always perpendicular to the incident ray
questions.explanation: The two laws are i = r and the coplanarity of the incident ray, normal and reflected ray. The angles do not have to add to 90°, nor are the rays always perpendicular.

questions.question: Two incident rays from different directions strike the SAME point on a mirror. Which of the following is the same for both?
options: The angle of reflection
The direction of the normal
The angle of incidence
The direction of the reflected ray
questions.explanation: The normal depends only on the point of incidence, so it is the same for both rays; their angles of incidence and reflected directions differ.

questions.question: The reflected ray from a plane mirror is found to be at right angles (90°) to the incident ray. The angle of incidence must be
questions.explanation: The angle between the rays is i + r = 2i. If 2i = 90°, then i = 45°.

questions.question: If the incident ray makes 30° with the mirror surface, the angle of reflection is 60°.
questions.explanation: True. Angle of incidence = 90° − 30° = 60° (measured from the normal), and the angle of reflection equals it: 60°.

questions.question: A student carefully records i = 30° and r = 31° in Table 10.1. The best conclusion is that
options: the law of reflection fails for this angle
the angle of reflection is always 1° larger
the mirror used must have been slightly convex
the angles are nearly equal, as the law predicts
questions.explanation: The chapter says the angles come out 'nearly equal' and, if done carefully, i = r. A 1° difference is drawing or measuring error, not a new law.

questions.question: A ray hits a plane mirror with angle of incidence 50°. Select the TWO correct values.
options: Angle of reflection = 50°
Angle between reflected ray and mirror = 40°
Angle between reflected ray and mirror = 50°
Angle between incident and reflected rays = 50°
questions.explanation: By the first law r = i = 50°. The reflected ray then makes 90° − 50° = 40° with the mirror, and the two rays are 100° apart.

questions.question: When multiple parallel beams of light fall on a PLANE mirror, the reflected beams are
options: also parallel to one another
brought closer to one another
spread apart from one another
reflected back along the same path
questions.explanation: Fig. 10.11b: parallel beams reflected from a plane mirror remain parallel.

questions.question: Parallel beams of light falling on a concave mirror, after reflection,
options: pass straight through the mirror
come closer, that is converge
spread out, that is diverge
remain parallel as before
questions.explanation: A concave mirror converges a parallel beam — the reflected beams get closer (Fig. 10.11c).

questions.question: After reflection from a convex mirror, parallel beams of light
options: stay parallel to each other
meet together at a single point
spread apart, that is diverge
get closer, that is converge
questions.explanation: A convex mirror diverges a parallel beam — the reflected beams spread out (Fig. 10.11d).

questions.question: How is Activity 10.6 different from Activity 10.4 in the way the comb is used?
options: Only one opening is left to get a single thin beam
The comb is replaced by a sheet of black chart paper
The comb is placed behind the mirror instead of in front
Many openings are left open to give several parallel beams
questions.explanation: In Activity 10.4 all but one slit is covered to obtain one beam; in Activity 10.6 many openings are left open to obtain multiple parallel beams.

questions.question: Each ray obeys the law i = r, yet parallel rays converge after reflecting from a concave mirror. Why?
options: The curved surface turns each ray by a different amount
The law of reflection does not hold for curved mirrors
Light slows down when it touches a curved surface
The rays are bent before they reach the mirror
questions.explanation: The chapter says that although each ray follows the laws of reflection, the curved surface of a spherical mirror causes the parallel rays to converge (concave) or diverge (convex).

questions.question: After reflecting from a convex mirror, parallel rays come closer together.
questions.explanation: False. A convex mirror diverges parallel rays — they spread apart. It is the concave mirror that makes them converge.

questions.question: A student shines several parallel beams on an unlabelled mirror and sees the reflected beams spreading apart. The mirror is
options: flat glass
convex
concave
plane
questions.explanation: Diverging reflected beams identify a convex mirror; a concave mirror converges them and a plane mirror keeps them parallel.

questions.question: The reflected beams from a mirror meet at a point in front of it. The mirror must be
options: plane
flat glass
concave
convex
questions.explanation: Only a concave mirror converges parallel beams so that they come together at a point.

questions.question: Select the TWO devices that CONVERGE a parallel beam of light.
options: Concave mirror
Convex lens
Convex mirror
Concave lens
questions.explanation: Concave mirrors and convex lenses converge light; convex mirrors and concave lenses diverge it.

questions.question: Which statement about mirrors and parallel beams is NOT correct?
options: A concave mirror converges a parallel beam of light
A plane mirror keeps a parallel beam parallel
A convex mirror diverges a parallel beam of light
A convex mirror converges a parallel beam of light
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors diverge light; the statement that they converge it is wrong. The other three statements match Fig. 10.11.

questions.question: A plane mirror neither converges nor diverges a parallel beam of light.
questions.explanation: True. Parallel beams stay parallel after reflecting from a plane mirror.

questions.question: In Activity 10.6 the same torch and comb are used with three different mirrors. Which is the variable being CHANGED?
options: The type of mirror
The number of beams
The brightness of the torch
The distance of the torch
questions.explanation: The multiple parallel beams are kept the same and only the mirror (plane, concave, convex) is swapped, so the mirror type is the variable being tested.

questions.question: In Activity 10.7 a concave mirror faces the Sun and its reflected light is directed onto a sheet of paper. After a few minutes the paper
options: shows an inverted image of the Sun
starts to burn, producing smoke
becomes cool and damp
becomes transparent like glass
questions.explanation: The concentrated sunlight produces enough heat at the bright spot to ignite the paper.

questions.question: Why does the paper catch fire at the bright spot formed by the concave mirror?
options: The reflected light is brighter than direct sunlight everywhere
The paper absorbs the mirror's aluminium coating
Sunlight is concentrated at one point, producing enough heat
The mirror itself becomes hot and touches the paper
questions.explanation: After reflection from the concave mirror the Sun's light gets concentrated at a point, and this concentration produces sufficient heat to ignite the paper.

questions.question: Which safety rule applies to Activity 10.7 with the concave mirror and the Sun?
options: Hold the paper as close to the mirror as possible
Do the activity indoors with a torch instead of the Sun
Wear gloves because the mirror becomes very hot
Do not look at the Sun or into the mirror reflecting it
questions.explanation: The Safety First box says: perform it under adult supervision, never look towards the Sun or into the reflecting mirror, and focus the light only on paper, never on anyone's face or eyes.

questions.question: Predict: Activity 10.7 is repeated with a CONVEX mirror of the same size. What happens?
options: No sharp bright spot forms, so the paper does not burn
The paper burns faster because the mirror is bigger
A bright spot forms farther from the mirror than before
The paper burns only if the mirror is held very close
questions.explanation: A convex mirror diverges the sunlight instead of concentrating it, so the light is spread out and cannot heat one point enough to ignite the paper.

questions.question: In Activity 10.11 the concave mirror is replaced by a convex lens in the path of the sunrays. The result is that the paper
options: shows a cool bright spot that does not heat up
can again be burnt, because the lens converges light
cannot be burnt, because lenses let light pass through
burns only on the side facing the Sun
questions.explanation: A convex lens converges the Sun's light to a bright spot just like a concave mirror does, so the paper can be burnt (Fig. 10.19).

questions.question: Devices that concentrate sunlight into a small area using mirrors and lenses are called
options: solar reflectors
solar generators
solar concentrators
solar collectors
questions.explanation: The 'A step further' box names such devices solar concentrators; the concentrated sunlight is used to heat a liquid.

questions.question: In a solar concentrator, the concentrated sunlight is used first to
options: charge a storage battery directly
melt the mirror into a lens
cool a liquid for cold storage
heat a liquid to produce steam
questions.explanation: The box explains that the concentrated sunlight heats a liquid to produce steam, which can generate electricity or supply heat for cooking or solar furnaces.

questions.question: Solar furnaces that concentrate sunlight are even used for melting steel.
questions.explanation: True. The chapter notes that solar furnaces are even used for melting steel, linking back to the earlier chapter on electric furnaces.

questions.question: In Activity 10.7 the paper should be held as close to the concave mirror as possible to get the brightest spot.
questions.explanation: False. The distance of the paper is ADJUSTED until a sharp bright spot forms; the light concentrates only at a particular distance from the mirror.

questions.question: In village solar cookers, mirrors are used to
options: converge sunlight to generate cooking heat
diverge the sunlight so the food cooks evenly
form an enlarged image of the food being cooked
store the sunlight for cooking after dark
questions.explanation: The 'Discover, design and debate' section says solar cookers use mirrors to converge sunlight and generate heat, saving electricity and fossil fuel.

questions.question: Select the TWO objects that can be used to burn a piece of paper with sunlight.
options: Concave mirror
Convex lens
Convex mirror
Concave lens
questions.explanation: Both the concave mirror (Activity 10.7) and the convex lens (Activity 10.11) converge sunlight to a hot bright spot. Convex mirrors and concave lenses diverge light.

questions.question: Why must the mirror and paper be held steady for a few minutes in Activity 10.7?
options: The paper must first dry out fully in the sunlight
Heat must build up at one point before the paper ignites
The mirror needs a few minutes to take a concave shape
The Sun must first move to a position directly overhead
questions.explanation: The concentrated spot heats a point; if the spot keeps moving, no single point gets hot enough. Holding steady lets heat accumulate until the paper burns.

questions.question: Which quantity is adjusted in Activity 10.7 to obtain a sharp bright spot on the paper?
options: The thickness of the sheet of paper
The colour of the sheet of paper used
The distance of the paper from the mirror
The angle of the Sun above the horizon
questions.explanation: The instruction is to adjust the distance of the paper until a sharp bright spot forms where the reflected sunlight concentrates.

questions.question: A lens is a piece of transparent material, usually glass or plastic, which has
options: a shiny coating
flat parallel faces
a dark backing
curved surfaces
questions.explanation: A lens is transparent and has curved surfaces; it is the curvature that changes how objects look through it.

questions.question: A lens that is thicker at the middle than at the edges is a
options: convex lens
concave lens
plane lens
convex mirror
questions.explanation: A convex lens is thicker in the middle (Fig. 10.15); a concave lens is thicker at the edges.

questions.question: A concave lens is
options: curved inwards on one side and flat on the other
thicker at the edges than at the middle
thicker at the middle than at the edges
equally thick at the middle and edges
questions.explanation: A lens which is thicker at the edges as compared to the middle is called a concave lens (Fig. 10.16).

questions.question: In Activity 10.8, why is a thin coating of oil or wax rubbed on the glass strip before placing the water drop?
options: It stops the water from magnifying the letters
It makes the letters under the strip darker
It helps the water form a nice round drop
It makes the glass strip act like a mirror
questions.explanation: The oil or wax prevents the water from spreading, so it forms a round, curved drop that can act like a lens.

questions.question: Letters seen through the water drop in Activity 10.8 look larger because the drop
options: reflects light like a tiny concave mirror
is made of a special magnifying liquid
makes the paper underneath swell up
is curved and acts like a simple lens
questions.explanation: The water drop's surface is curved outwards; this curved transparent drop acts like a simple lens and changes the apparent size of the text.

questions.question: Objects seen through a flat transparent window pane look the same size and shape. Why does a water drop on glass behave differently?
options: The drop's surface is curved, the pane's is flat
The drop is a liquid while the pane is a solid
The drop reflects light while the pane transmits it
The drop is much thinner than the pane of glass
questions.explanation: It is the curvature of the transparent surface that changes the apparent size of objects; a flat pane leaves them unchanged.

questions.question: What is the key difference between how we use a mirror and a lens?
options: A lens forms images but a mirror does not
We see things through a lens but in a mirror
We see things in a lens but through a mirror
A lens is transparent but a mirror is curved
questions.explanation: Unlike mirrors, lenses allow light to pass through them, so we see things THROUGH a lens rather than IN it.

questions.question: A magnifying glass is a lens that helps in reading small print by making the letters appear bigger.
questions.explanation: True. The chapter introduces the magnifying glass (Fig. 10.14) as a lens that makes letters appear bigger.

questions.question: A concave lens is thicker in the middle than at its edges.
questions.explanation: False. A concave lens is thicker at the edges; it is the convex lens that is thicker in the middle.

questions.question: The surface of the water drop in Activity 10.8 is
options: perfectly flat
flat on top and curved below
curved outwards
curved inwards
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the surface of the water drop is curved outside, which is why it behaves like a convex-type lens.

questions.question: A student first looks at text through a flat plastic scale (same size) and then through a water drop on the scale (larger). Which variable changed between the two observations?
options: The transparency of the material
The size of the printed letters
The distance of the eye from the text
The curvature of the transparent surface
questions.explanation: Both the scale and the drop are transparent and the text is unchanged; what differs is the curved surface of the drop, which is what makes it act as a lens.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements that are true of every lens.
options: It is made of a transparent material
It has curved surfaces
It reflects light back from its front face
It is thicker at the edges than the middle
questions.explanation: All lenses are transparent with curved surfaces. Reflecting from the front is a mirror property, and being thicker at the edges describes only concave lenses.

questions.question: Like mirrors, lenses can also be
options: convex or concave
shiny or dull
plane or spherical
opaque or transparent
questions.explanation: The chapter says: 'Like mirrors, lenses can also be convex or concave', defined by whether they are thicker at the middle or at the edges.

questions.question: Which statement about lenses is NOT correct?
options: A lens has surfaces that are curved, not flat
A lens needs a reflective coating on one side
A lens is usually made of glass or plastic
A lens allows light to pass through it
questions.explanation: Lenses are transparent and work by letting light pass through; a reflective coating is what mirrors have.

questions.question: An object placed close behind a convex lens and seen through it appears
options: inverted and enlarged
inverted and diminished
erect and enlarged
erect and diminished
questions.explanation: At a small distance behind a convex lens the object appears erect and enlarged — this is how a magnifying glass works.

questions.question: As the distance between an object and a convex lens is increased, the object seen through the lens
options: stays erect but becomes smaller and smaller
appears inverted and the same size throughout
stays erect and keeps on becoming larger and larger
appears inverted, first enlarged and then smaller
questions.explanation: As the distance increases the object appears inverted; it is initially enlarged and then diminishes in size — the same pattern as the concave mirror.

questions.question: An object seen through a concave lens always appears
options: erect and diminished
erect and enlarged
inverted and diminished
inverted and enlarged
questions.explanation: An object placed behind a concave lens always appears erect and smaller in size, though its size changes with distance.

questions.question: A pen cap is placed at the same distance behind a convex lens, a concave lens and a flat glass piece. Image (i) is the same size, (ii) is enlarged, (iii) is diminished. The matching is
options: (i) concave lens, (ii) convex lens, (iii) flat glass
(i) flat glass, (ii) convex lens, (iii) concave lens
(i) flat glass, (ii) concave lens, (iii) convex lens
(i) convex lens, (ii) flat glass, (iii) concave lens
questions.explanation: Flat glass leaves the size unchanged, a convex lens enlarges a nearby object, and a concave lens always diminishes it.

questions.question: A magnifying glass held near a page shows the text bigger. As it is moved slowly away from the page, the text
options: becomes gradually smaller but remains erect
disappears because the lens stops working at a distance
becomes inverted, first enlarged then smaller
keeps on growing larger and remains erect
questions.explanation: A magnifying glass is a convex lens: a nearby object appears erect and enlarged, but as the distance grows the object appears inverted, first enlarged then diminished.

questions.question: 'Object placed behind it may appear inverted at some distance.' This describes which item?
options: Concave lens
Convex mirror
Flat glass plate
Convex lens
questions.explanation: Only the convex lens (among lenses) inverts the object once it is far enough away; a concave lens always shows it erect.

questions.question: 'Object placed behind it always appears diminished in size.' This describes which item?
options: Concave lens
Convex lens
Concave mirror
Magnifying glass
questions.explanation: A concave lens always gives an erect, diminished view. A convex lens (a magnifying glass) can enlarge, and a concave mirror is not something you look through.

questions.question: Which statement about objects viewed through a concave lens is NOT correct?
options: Their apparent size changes with distance
They appear inverted when far from the lens
They always appear erect, never upside down
They always appear smaller than they are
questions.explanation: A concave lens never inverts; the object always appears erect and diminished, although its apparent size changes as the distance increases.

questions.question: An object seen through a concave lens always appears erect.
questions.explanation: True. The chapter states that an object behind a concave lens always appears erect and diminished.

questions.question: An object seen through a convex lens always appears enlarged.
questions.explanation: False. A convex lens enlarges a nearby object, but as the distance increases the object appears inverted and eventually diminished.

questions.question: Which LENS shows the same pattern of image changes as a CONCAVE MIRROR (erect and enlarged when near, inverted when far)?
options: Both lenses
Neither lens
Convex lens
Concave lens
questions.explanation: The convex lens behaves like the concave mirror: erect enlarged for a near object, inverted (first enlarged, then smaller) for a far one.

questions.question: Which LENS behaves like a CONVEX MIRROR, always giving an erect and diminished view?
options: Convex lens
Magnifying glass
Flat glass piece
Concave lens
questions.explanation: A concave lens, like a convex mirror, always shows the object erect and smaller. A magnifying glass is a convex lens and flat glass does not change size.

questions.question: Select the TWO optical devices whose images are ALWAYS erect and diminished.
options: Convex mirror
Concave lens
Concave mirror
Convex lens
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors and concave lenses always give erect, diminished images; concave mirrors and convex lenses give images that depend on object distance.

questions.question: Column I lists (i) concave mirror, (ii) convex mirror, (iii) convex lens, (iv) concave lens. Column II lists (a) curves inwards, (b) always erect and diminished image, (c) object may appear inverted at some distance, (d) object always appears diminished. The correct matching is
questions.explanation: A concave mirror curves inwards; a convex mirror always gives an erect diminished image; a convex lens can show an object inverted at a distance; a concave lens always shows it diminished.

questions.question: The apparent size of an object seen through a concave lens stays exactly the same at every distance.
questions.explanation: False. Although always erect and diminished, the chapter notes its size changes as the distance from the lens increases.

questions.question: In Activity 10.9 the SAME object is viewed through a convex lens and then a concave lens at increasing distances. What is the control (kept the same) in this comparison?
options: The orientation of the image
The object being viewed
The type of lens used
The apparent size of the image
questions.explanation: The object is kept the same and only the lens is swapped, so differences in image size and orientation can be attributed to the lens.

questions.question: A convex lens is also called a
options: magnifying mirror
plane lens
converging lens
diverging lens
questions.explanation: A convex lens converges the light falling on it, so it is also called a converging lens.

questions.question: Because of what it does to a parallel beam of light, a concave lens is called a
options: converging lens
focusing lens
reflecting lens
diverging lens
questions.explanation: A concave lens spreads out (diverges) the light passing through it, so it is called a diverging lens.

questions.question: In Activity 10.10 multiple parallel beams pass through a thin transparent glass plate. The beams
options: pass through unchanged, still parallel
converge to a point behind the plate
diverge slightly after the plate
are reflected back towards the torch
questions.explanation: The light beam passes through the thin glass plate as it is; only the curved lenses converge or diverge it (Fig. 10.18a).

questions.question: Predict: parallel beams of light are sent through a concave lens. On the paper beyond the lens the beams will
options: turn back towards the torch that sent them
spread farther apart from each other
come together at one bright point
remain exactly parallel to one another
questions.explanation: A concave lens diverges light, so the beams spread apart after passing through it (Fig. 10.18c).

questions.question: The eyeglasses people wear to see clearly are
options: concave mirrors
flat glass plates
pairs of lenses
plane mirrors
questions.explanation: The chapter lists eyeglasses as an everyday use of lenses (Fig. 10.20a).

questions.question: Which group of devices does the chapter say all use lenses to work?
options: Torches, headlights and dental mirrors
Side-view mirrors and road-bend mirrors
Solar furnaces, steel furnaces and heaters
Cameras, telescopes and microscopes
questions.explanation: Cameras, telescopes and microscopes all use lenses. Torch reflectors and dental mirrors are concave mirrors; side-view and road mirrors are convex mirrors.

questions.question: The lens inside the human eye is special because it
options: can change shape to see near and far objects
is concave and always diminishes images
is flat like a transparent window pane
reflects light like a concave mirror
questions.explanation: The chapter says our eye has a convex lens that can change its shape, which lets us read a book and also see something far away.

questions.question: Our eye contains a convex lens that can change its shape.
questions.explanation: True. The eye's convex lens changes shape so that we can read nearby text or see distant objects clearly.

questions.question: A concave lens is also known as a converging lens.
questions.explanation: False. A concave lens diverges light and is called a diverging lens; the converging lens is the convex lens.

questions.question: Select the TWO devices that DIVERGE a parallel beam of light.
options: Convex mirror
Concave lens
Concave mirror
Convex lens
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors and concave lenses spread light out; concave mirrors and convex lenses bring it together.

questions.question: Which statement about Activity 10.10 is NOT correct?
options: A thin flat glass plate lets light pass as it is
A thin flat glass plate converges light slightly
A convex lens converges light
A concave lens diverges light
questions.explanation: Activity 10.10 shows the thin glass plate passes the parallel beam unchanged; it neither converges nor diverges. Convex lenses converge and concave lenses diverge.

questions.question: A convex lens does to a light beam what which mirror does?
options: Plane mirror
Side-view mirror
Concave mirror
Convex mirror
questions.explanation: Both the convex lens and the concave mirror converge a parallel beam of light.

questions.question: In Activity 10.10 the glass plate, convex lens and concave lens are tested one by one with the same torch and comb. What is kept the same and what is changed?
options: Same: the transparent object; changed: the beam angle
Same: the number of beams; changed: the torch brightness
Same: the lens; changed: the number of books
Same: the parallel beams; changed: the transparent object
questions.explanation: The parallel beams from the torch and comb are the fixed input; swapping the plate, convex lens and concave lens is the variable whose effect is observed.

questions.question: Fig. 10.20b shows the camera lenses on a smartphone. This illustrates that
options: cameras use lenses to work
cameras use concave mirrors to work
smartphones use plane mirrors to focus
cameras work with flat glass plates only
questions.explanation: The figure is given as an example of lenses used in cameras, alongside eyeglasses.

questions.question: More than 800 years ago, during the time of Bhāskara II, Indian astronomers observed stars and planets using
options: hollow metal spheres
shallow bowls of water
polished bronze mirrors
glass convex lenses
questions.explanation: The 'Our scientific heritage' box says astronomers used shallow bowls of water and observed the reflected images of stars and planets.

questions.question: How did those ancient astronomers use the reflected images in the water bowls?
options: They used them to burn paper and tell the time of day
They used them to magnify the planets for drawing maps
They viewed them through angled tubes to measure positions
They photographed them to keep a record of the night sky
questions.explanation: By carefully looking at the reflected images through tubes placed at appropriate angles they could measure the positions of stars and planets.

questions.question: What does the chapter conclude about the ancient astronomers and the laws of reflection?
options: They wrote down both laws of reflection exactly as we state them today
They knew only the first law of reflection and not the second one
They did not make use of reflection at all in their observations
Not written in their texts, yet their methods show practical understanding
questions.explanation: The box says that although the laws of reflection are not mentioned in the literature, their instruments and methods indicate they might have understood them in practice.

questions.question: Ancient Indian astronomers of Bhāskara II's time described the laws of reflection in detail in their written works.
questions.explanation: False. The chapter says the laws of reflection are NOT mentioned in their literature; their instruments merely suggest a practical understanding.

questions.question: A pencil stands behind a transparent tumbler that is half filled with water. Through the water-filled part the pencil appears different in size from the part above the water. The best explanation is that
options: the curved water-filled tumbler acts like a lens
water reflects the pencil like a mirror
the pencil has actually bent inside the water
the glass tumbler blocks some of the light
questions.explanation: The water in the curved tumbler is a transparent material with a curved surface — just like the water drop in Activity 10.8 — so it acts like a lens and changes how the pencil looks.

questions.question: 'Can we make mirrors which give enlarged or diminished images?' Based on this chapter, the answer is
options: Yes — a convex mirror enlarges and a concave mirror diminishes
Yes — a concave mirror can enlarge and a convex mirror diminishes
No — every mirror forms an image the same size as the object
Yes — but only a plane mirror can enlarge the image
questions.explanation: Spherical mirrors change image size: a concave mirror gives an enlarged image for a near object, while a convex mirror always gives a diminished one.

questions.question: Using designs like solar cookers in Indian villages helps society mainly by
options: allowing cooking without any sunlight
replacing all electric furnaces in factories
saving electricity and reducing fossil fuel use
making concave mirrors cheaper to buy
questions.explanation: The 'Discover, design and debate' section says such solar cooker designs save electricity and reduce fossil fuel use.

questions.question: The still water surface in the astronomers' shallow bowl formed a reflected image of a star. Because the surface was flat, it behaved most like a
options: concave mirror
convex mirror
convex lens
plane mirror
questions.explanation: A flat reflecting surface behaves like a plane mirror, forming an erect, same-size image of what is above it.

questions.question: A dentist's mirror and a vehicle's side-view mirror are the same type of spherical mirror.
questions.explanation: False. The dental mirror is concave (gives an enlarged view of a nearby tooth) while the side-view mirror is convex (gives a wide, erect, diminished view).
